description: Paper categories, ISO sizes, gsm and microns, plus boards used in everyday design.
content_html:
From Wood Pulp to Printed Page

Paper and board are among the oldest industrial materials, yet they remain central to modern design—from product packaging to architectural models. Both begin as wood pulp, produced either mechanically (grinding logs into fibres) or chemically (using reagents to dissolve lignin and release clean cellulose). Chemical pulp produces stronger, longer-lasting sheets; mechanical pulp is cheaper but yellows over time because lignin remains in the fibres.

Paper is measured in two ways. Grammage (gsm) describes mass per unit area. Copy paper is typically 80 gsm; a premium business card may be 350 gsm. Microns describe physical thickness: standard copy paper sits around 100 microns. The two figures usually move together, but coated papers can be heavier per micron than uncoated ones because the coating adds density without adding much bulk.

Key Fact

Paper weight is measured in gsm (grams per square metre); paper thickness is measured in microns. Standard copy paper is around 80 gsm and approximately 100 microns thick. Card and board start at roughly 200 gsm.

ISO Paper Sizes

The international standard for paper sizing is the ISO 216 series. The A-series is built on a single mathematical relationship: each size is exactly half the area of the one above it, and the aspect ratio remains constant at 1:√2 (approximately 1:1.414). This means an A3 sheet folded in half gives two A4 sheets, an A4 folded in half gives two A5 sheets, and so on. A0 has an area of exactly 1 m². Designers use this relationship routinely when scaling artwork: an image laid out on A3 will reproduce correctly at A4 without distortion.

The B-series covers intermediate sizes (useful for posters and passports), and the C-series is used for envelopes (a C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat). In practice, the A-series is what designers, printers and students encounter daily.

The most commonly used A-series sizes in design and education:

SizeDimensions (mm)Typical use
A0841 × 1189Large posters, architectural drawings
A1594 × 841Exhibition posters, flip chart pads
A2420 × 594Technical drawings, display boards
A3297 × 420Design sheets, presentation boards
A4210 × 297Letters, standard printing
A5148 × 210Leaflets, notebooks
A6105 × 148Postcards, pocket notebooks

Types of Paper

Layout paper is thin and slightly translucent—ideal for developing ideas quickly in pencil. Designers layer sheets over earlier sketches to refine forms without starting from scratch. Tracing paper is more transparent still, used to copy existing drawings accurately. Cartridge paper is the general-purpose drawing paper used in most D&T studios: heavier than layout paper (typically 100–140 gsm), with a slightly textured surface that holds pencil and ink well. Bleed-proof paper has an extra smooth coating that stops alcohol-based markers bleeding through to the sheet beneath.

Recycled paper is made from post-consumer waste fibres that have been de-inked and re-pulped. Each recycling cycle shortens the fibres slightly, which reduces strength over successive cycles, but modern paper can contain 100% recycled content for many applications. Recycled paper typically has a slightly grey or cream tint rather than the bright white of virgin-fibre sheets, because optical brightening agents (OBAs) are harder to apply uniformly to recycled pulp.

Types of Board

Boards are heavier-duty sheets, generally above 200 gsm, produced by laminating multiple paper layers together or using a thicker single-ply process. The main boards used in GCSE D&T are:

  • Corrugated board—a sandwich of flat liners bonded to a fluted inner layer. The fluting creates a rigid structure that is surprisingly light. Used in protective transit packaging and models. Typically 3 mm to 5 mm thick but weighs far less than solid card of the same thickness.
  • Folding boxboard (FBB)—a multi-layer board with a white coated surface ideal for high-quality printing. Used in cereal boxes, medicine packets and cosmetic packaging. The inner layers may contain mechanical pulp to reduce cost, with a chemical-pulp surface layer for printability.
  • Mounting board—a thick, rigid board (1.5–3 mm) used to mount and present artwork or photographs. Available in many colours. Commonly used by designers to present rendered illustrations or to produce scale architectural models.
Key Fact

Corrugated board achieves rigidity through its fluted inner layer sandwiched between flat liners. Folding boxboard (FBB) is the standard for printed retail packaging. Mounting board is rigid presentation-quality board used to display artwork and build scale models.

Laminating and Finishing

Laminating applies a thin plastic film (typically polypropylene) to a printed sheet. Gloss laminate intensifies colour and reflects light; matt laminate reduces glare and gives a softer feel. Both significantly improve the product’s resistance to moisture, tearing and everyday handling. Laminating is common on book covers, loyalty cards and food packaging where the printed surface must survive repeated handling.

Other finishes include spot UV varnish (a glossy coating applied to specific areas only to create contrast), embossing (pressing a design into the board to create a raised surface) and foil blocking (applying a metallic foil under heat and pressure). Each adds cost and requires specialist equipment, but can significantly increase the perceived quality of a product.

The 12-mark extended response question asks you to demonstrate depth in ONE chosen material area. For papers and boards, top-band answers include: specific named paper or board types (not just “cardboard”), precise properties linked to application (e.g. folding boxboard’s coated surface enables high-quality litho printing for retail packaging), and at least one sustainability point (e.g. recycled content, biodegradable vs laminated boards at end of life). The weakest answers say “card is strong and light” without naming a specific board type or linking properties to a product context.

A strong Q6 paragraph on papers and boards might read: “Folding boxboard is used for cereal packaging because its multi-layer construction combines a smooth, coated outer surface for litho printing with mechanical-pulp inner layers that reduce cost. At end of life, unlaminated FBB is recyclable and biodegradable, making it preferable to plastics for mass-market retail packaging.” Note: three specific facts, a process link, and an environmental evaluation in one short paragraph.
exam_tip_html: In questions about papers and boards, always name the specific paper or board type rather than writing “paper” or “cardboard” — examiners reward precision. If a question asks about properties, link the property directly to a product application (for example: “corrugated board’s fluted structure gives rigidity for transit packaging without adding excessive weight”). For 6-mark and 12-mark questions, include at least one sustainability or end-of-life point, such as recyclability vs laminated boards, to access the highest marks. Remember: for the 12-mark Q6, answer ONE material area in depth — attempting more than one means only the first is marked.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Paper and board both derive from wood pulp (mechanical or chemical). Weight is measured in gsm; thickness in microns. Standard copy paper is around 80 gsm / 100 microns; board starts at roughly 200 gsm.
  • ISO A-series sizes halve in area at each step (A3 = half of A2), with a constant 1:√2 aspect ratio. A4 is the everyday standard; A0 has an area of 1 m².
  • Key boards: corrugated board (fluted core, rigid and light), folding boxboard (coated, printable, retail packaging), mounting board (rigid, presentation-quality). Laminating adds a plastic film to improve durability and water resistance.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what gsm measures in relation to paper?
A) The physical thickness of the paper in millimetres
B) The number of sheets in a ream
C) The mass of one square metre of paper in grams
D) The ratio of paper width to height
practice_questions.marks: C) The mass of one square metre of paper in grams [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the dimensions of an A4 sheet of paper.
practice_questions.marks: 210 mm wide [1 mark] and 297 mm tall [1 mark]. (Both dimensions required for 2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Describe two properties of corrugated board that make it suitable for transit packaging.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks from:
• Rigid structure due to the fluted inner layer, which resists crushing [1]
• Lightweight relative to its thickness because the fluting creates air pockets [1]
• Provides cushioning and impact protection [1]
• Recyclable / made from recycled content [1]
(1 mark per valid property with brief reason; max 3)

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose folding boxboard rather than plain card for a retail cereal box.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Folding boxboard has a coated outer surface [1] which allows high-quality litho printing for graphics and branding [1]
• The multi-layer construction gives stiffness [1] so the box holds its shape on a shelf [1]
• The chemical-pulp outer layer produces a brighter white surface than mechanical pulp [1] which makes colours appear more vivid [1]
(2 marks per developed point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: Explain, with reference to a specific product, why manufacturers sometimes apply a laminate finish to printed board packaging. Include in your answer one potential disadvantage of laminating.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific product (e.g. paperback book cover, loyalty card, food carton), explains how laminating improves durability and water resistance in that context with a developed mechanism (e.g. polypropylene film prevents moisture penetration in a chilled food box), and evaluates a genuine disadvantage (e.g. laminate prevents the board from being recycled through standard paper streams, reducing end-of-life sustainability).
Secure: Names a product and explains one benefit of laminating with some product-specific detail, plus identifies one disadvantage.
Developing: General explanation of laminating benefits without product-specific application; disadvantage may be vague.
Emerging: Superficial statement about laminating with no product context or disadvantage.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using recycled paper rather than virgin-fibre paper for an office printing paper product. Consider both performance and environmental factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides. Advantages may include: lower energy and water use in production, reduced demand on virgin timber, lower carbon footprint, can be certified under recognised schemes. Disadvantages may include: shorter fibre length reduces tensile strength with each recycle cycle, potential grey/cream tint reducing brightness, possible de-inking residues, OBAs harder to apply uniformly. Reaches a reasoned judgement about which factors weigh more heavily for the specific product context.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with some product-specific detail; judgement present but may lack full development.
Developing: Points identified on both sides but limited development; judgement weak or absent.
Emerging: Only one side addressed or points are superficial.

knowledge_checks.q: What does gsm stand for when describing paper weight?
Which type of board uses a fluted inner layer between two flat liners to achieve rigidity?
Standard copy paper is typically _____ gsm.
In the ISO A-series, each size is exactly _____ the area of the size above it.
Match each paper or board type to its primary use:
right: Developing design ideas through overlaying sketches
Retail packaging requiring high-quality printed surfaces
Presenting artwork or building scale models

flashcard_questions.q: What unit is used to measure paper weight (mass per area)?
What unit measures the physical thickness of paper?
Standard office copy paper is typically _____ gsm.
What is the area of an A0 sheet?
What are the dimensions of an A4 sheet?
How does an A3 sheet relate in size to an A4 sheet?
flashcard_questions.a: A3 is exactly double the area of A4.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes corrugated board rigid despite being lightweight?
flashcard_questions.a: A fluted inner layer sandwiched between two flat liners.

flashcard_questions.q: Which board type has a coated outer surface for high-quality printing on retail packaging?
What is layout paper used for in design?
flashcard_questions.a: Developing ideas quickly by overlaying sketches.

flashcard_questions.q: What process bonds a thin plastic film to a printed sheet to improve durability?
Why does recycled paper often appear slightly grey or cream rather than bright white?
flashcard_questions.a: Optical brightening agents are harder to apply uniformly to recycled pulp.

flashcard_questions.q: Chemical pulp vs mechanical pulp — which produces stronger, longer-lasting paper?
What is the environmental disadvantage of applying a laminate finish to board packaging?
flashcard_questions.a: The plastic film prevents the board from being recycled through standard paper streams.

glossary_terms.definition: Cellulose fibres extracted from wood or recycled waste and processed into sheets for writing, printing or packaging.
Grams per square metre — the standard measure of paper weight and thickness used across the industry.
A lightweight, semi-transparent paper used for overlaying and tracing design drawings.
Bonding a thin plastic film to a printed sheet to improve durability, water resistance and appearance.
